reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it reports and tests allegations that OneCoin lacked a functioning blockchain and was connected to criminal activity, rather than promoting participation in OneCoin. The speakers describe conducting account and transaction tests, cooperating with authorities, and stopping their own promotion of the business. No viewer payment, data submission, purchase, recruitment, or other consequential action is requested.

citations.quote: I'm not a OneCorner, but I have been following this case for a long time. I'm working with the authorities
we've done multiple tests for mining for sending just transactions back and forth and so on
I can't promote this business anymore
None of them are recorded in the blockchain, in the visible blockchain that we can see
everyone here can try a small transaction from one account to another account just send one coin

opening.argument: The discussion supplies a concrete action path involving the asset itself: viewers are told they can send a small amount from one account to another, then inspect later blocks. The speaker further says that, if approved, the transaction should be written into the blockchain. That links transferring OneCoin to a promised verification outcome. Even presented as a test, it normalizes sending the asset and invites viewers to participate in the system being evaluated. The absence of a conventional purchase pitch does not eliminate the acquisition mechanism: the viewer is still encouraged to handle and transfer the digital asset in order to obtain confidence in the claimed blockchain.

citations.quote: everyone here can try a small transaction from one account to another account just send one coin
Then go back to the blockchain and read the blocks from before you sent the transactions
as soon as they're approved, they are written into the blockchain

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the transfer a test does not remove the action pathway. The speaker directly tells the audience to send one coin and explains what result they should expect afterward. The defense's claim that no consequential action is requested therefore overlooks the explicit invitation to transfer the asset, even if the stated purpose is verification.

citations.quote: everyone here can try a small transaction from one account to another account just send one coin
as soon as they're approved, they are written into the blockchain

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted instruction is an investigative test, not a promise of a free reward or asset acquisition. It asks viewers to send a small amount only to check whether a transaction appears. The speaker's reported result is the opposite of a successful promotional pathway: he says the transactions were not recorded in the visible blockchain.

citations.quote: we've done multiple tests for mining for sending just transactions back and forth and so on
None of them are recorded in the blockchain, in the visible blockchain that we can see

opening.argument: The video concentrates several unusually serious signals around money and a digital asset: viewers are told they paid money into an organization accused of hiding it, the speaker describes a large proposed salary, and the system is tested through repeated account transfers. The speaker also says transactions lacked both a transaction ID and a precise timestamp. Together, those details portray an opaque asset system in which money enters an organization while basic transaction verification is missing. That combination is consistent with a low-barrier asset-acquisition scheme whose apparent technical infrastructure cannot independently substantiate what happened to participants' funds.

citations.quote: you've actually paid money into an organization that is known for at the highest levels of hiding that money and using that for activities that are not legal
they proposed a large salary
None of them are recorded in the blockchain, in the visible blockchain that we can see
I did not get a transaction ID
i didn't get a timestamp

rebuttal.rebuttal: The warning framing does not neutralize the underlying risk signals; it makes them the subject of a highly persuasive account of a money-holding organization and an allegedly nonfunctional blockchain. The defense points to investigation, but the speaker's description of missing transaction identifiers, timestamps, and records is itself the reason viewers could be misled about what their asset transfers represent.

citations.quote: I did not get a transaction ID
i didn't get a timestamp
None of them are recorded in the blockchain, in the visible blockchain that we can see

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are allegations and test results presented as reasons for caution, not signals that viewers should acquire an asset. The video explicitly reports that money was allegedly hidden and that transactions could not be traced, which undermines rather than supports a promise of successful acquisition or reward. A large proposed salary is unrelated to a viewer return.

citations.quote: I'm working with the authorities
there's no connection to any of the transactions that we perform
they proposed a large salary

opening.argument: Although the speakers present themselves as critics, the program repeatedly centers the OneCoin business, its blockchain, its accounts, its transactions, and how to test them. One speaker confirms that he previously pitched the business, while another explains that he was recruited as a global CTO and had been offered a large salary. This insider-centered presentation can function as promotional exposure: it gives the scheme sustained technical attention and a participation-oriented test for viewers. The later criticism does not erase the practical effect of directing attention toward the asset and showing viewers how to interact with its accounts.

citations.quote: I pitched the business believing there was a blockchain
recruitment company called me for recruitment to be the global CTO of OneCoin
they proposed a large salary
everyone here can try a small transaction from one account to another account just send one coin

rebuttal.rebuttal: The apparent warning can still promote attention and engagement with the asset by explaining its accounts, blockchain, and transaction procedure. The speakers' former roles and technical credentials give the presentation authority, while the audience is told how to perform a OneCoin transfer. Thus the content does not need to praise the scheme explicitly to steer viewers toward interacting with it.

citations.quote: I pitched the business believing there was a blockchain
everyone here can try a small transaction from one account to another account just send one coin

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The speakers' former involvement is disclosed as background for explaining why they rejected the business, not as an endorsement. One speaker expressly says he cannot promote it anymore, and the other reports that none of the tested transactions appeared in the visible blockchain. Those statements direct viewers away from participation rather than toward it.
